identity.title: Food Safety Plan (Preventive Controls for Human Food): ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips, Salem plant
identity.issuer: Willamette Valley Foods, Inc. (prepared by Dana Whitfield, Quality Manager and PCQI)
identity.site: Salem — 1850 Fairgrounds Road NE, Salem, Oregon 97301

scan.summary: This is your written food safety plan for the Salem plant, which FDA's Preventive Controls rule (21 CFR 117, Subpart C) requires. It covers the hazard analysis, preventive controls, monitoring, corrective actions, verification, the supply-chain program, records and training. The plan has a workable outline, but important parts are missing or thin. There is no signature, no recall plan, no validation, no reanalysis schedule and no refrigerated-storage control. Salmonella from tahini added after the cook is not handled, and the supply-chain and environmental monitoring procedures are incomplete. The cook limit as written may not be reachable at all.
scan.freshness_note: The plan took effect May 12, 2025, so it is about 16 months old. The rule requires a reanalysis at least every 3 years, which means by May 12, 2028. It also requires one sooner if a product, process, ingredient or supplier changes, or if a control is found not to work. The plan names no reanalysis date, so ask whether a later revision exists.

gaps.title: Stones in dry beans have no working control
gaps.description: The hazard analysis says stones in dry beans are controlled by metal detection and supplier screening. A metal detector does not find stones. Supplier screening is not written up as a supply-chain control, and no monitoring or verification is set for it.
gaps.fix: Add a working control for stones, such as a destoner or visual sorting at receiving or soaking, with monitoring and corrective actions. Or write up the supplier screening as a supply-chain-applied control with verification under Subpart G.
gaps.locator: Section 3, Hazard analysis, row 'Receiving dry beans'
gaps.quote: Field debris in dry beans, controlled at metal detection and by supplier screening

gaps.title: Plan is not signed and dated by the owner, operator or agent in charge
gaps.description: The cover says only 'Approved by: Plant Manager'. There is no name, no signature and no date. The rule requires the owner, operator or agent in charge to sign and date the plan when it is first completed and again after any change.
gaps.fix: Have the owner, operator or agent in charge sign and date the plan now, and add a revision and signature block for future changes.

gaps.title: Corrective actions leave out required steps
gaps.description: Most corrective actions only deal with the product. They do not say how the cause will be found and fixed, how a repeat will be prevented, or how affected food will be evaluated and kept out of commerce. Examples: cooling failure, ATP failure, metal detector failure, label mismatch. There is also no corrective action for a positive finished-product Listeria test, and none for an unanticipated problem.
gaps.fix: For each control, add these steps: find and correct the cause, prevent a repeat, evaluate affected food, and keep adulterated food out of commerce. Add a procedure for a positive product test and a general procedure under 117.150(b) for problems the plan does not anticipate.
gaps.quote: If cooling exceeds the time limits, the batch is discarded.

gaps.title: No reanalysis schedule or triggers
gaps.description: The plan does not say it will be reanalyzed at least every 3 years. It also does not name the events that call for a reanalysis sooner: a change in product, process, ingredient or supplier, new hazard information, an unanticipated problem, or a control that is found not to work.
gaps.fix: Add a reanalysis section with the 3-year cycle, the triggering events, and who (the PCQI) performs or oversees it.

gaps.title: Hazard analysis leaves out chemical hazards and some biological ones
gaps.description: The hazard analysis has no chemical hazards at all. Examples it would normally weigh: pesticide residues or mycotoxins in beans, sanitizer residues, and allergen cross-contact from other ingredients such as spices. It also does not address Salmonella in tahini. Nor does it address Clostridium botulinum in a sealed, refrigerated low-acid dip with a 45-day shelf life, since no pH or acidity control is described. Not every step is evaluated: garlic, lemon juice and spices at receiving are not looked at, and neither are filling and sealing.
gaps.fix: Evaluate every step for biological, chemical and physical hazards, and record why each one does or does not need a preventive control. Add the missing hazards to Sections 3 and 4.

gaps.title: Label check at packaging is not monitored, and neither are allergen changeovers
gaps.description: The allergen control calls for label review at receipt and at printing, plus a washdown checked by ATP swab before the next product without sesame. Monitoring covers only the label review at receipt. Nothing checks that the right label is on the right product at filling or coding. Nothing records the scheduling order or the washdown and ATP result at the sesame changeover.
gaps.fix: Add monitoring for the label check at packaging or start-up and for each changeover washdown, with the ATP result. Add matching corrective actions for a wrong label on product and a failed changeover.
gaps.locator: Section 4 (Sesame allergen row) and Section 5, Monitoring
gaps.quote: The quality technician reviews every label lot against the formulation sheet at receipt and signs the label log.

gaps.title: Salmonella in tahini and other ingredients added after the cook is not addressed
gaps.description: Only the beans are cooked. Tahini, garlic, lemon juice, spices and oil are blended in after the kill step. Tahini has a known Salmonella history. The plan names no preventive control for these ingredients, and no supply-chain-applied control for them.
gaps.fix: Add these hazards to the hazard analysis. Control them with a supply-chain-applied control, such as supplier verification plus pathogen testing or a certificate of analysis tied to a validated supplier kill step, with verification under 117.410. A later process step could also serve as the control.

gaps.title: Cold storage is listed as needing a control, but there is no control, monitoring or corrective action
gaps.description: The hazard analysis marks Listeria growth in refrigerated storage as needing a preventive control. Section 4 has no storage temperature control, Section 5 has no cooler temperature monitoring, and Section 6 has no corrective action for a temperature excursion.
gaps.fix: Add a refrigeration control (41°F or below), continuous or scheduled cooler temperature monitoring, and corrective actions for excursions, with the product held and evaluated.
gaps.locator: Section 3, row 'Refrigerated storage'; missing from Sections 4–6
gaps.quote: Refrigerated RTE product with a 45-day shelf life

gaps.title: Cooling monitoring does not record when the clock starts
gaps.description: The limit is 135°F to 70°F in 2 hours and then to 41°F in 4 more hours. The log records the temperature at 2 hours and at 6 hours, but not the time and temperature when cooling starts at 135°F. Without that, neither time limit can be shown to have been met.
gaps.fix: Record the start time and temperature (at or above 135°F), then the temperature and time at 2 hours and 6 hours, and the operator's initials.
gaps.quote: The blast chiller operator records the temperature at 2 hours and at 6 hours on the cooling log.

gaps.title: Supply-chain program is missing required elements
gaps.description: The section is two sentences long. It does not say which hazards the suppliers control. It does not explain how suppliers are approved, how the verification activities and their frequency were chosen, or how certificates of analysis are checked. It covers no ingredients beyond tahini and beans, and it does not list the supply-chain records to be kept.
gaps.fix: Write out the program: which ingredients have supplier-controlled hazards, how suppliers are approved, the chosen verification activities and why, and how to receive from approved suppliers only. Include the records kept under 117.475.
gaps.quote: Tahini and dry beans are received only from approved suppliers who provide a current third-party audit certificate and a certificate of analysis for each lot.

gaps.title: No written recall plan
gaps.description: The plan has hazards that need preventive controls, so it must include a written recall plan. There is none. It should cover how direct customers are notified, public notice, effectiveness checks, and what happens to recalled product.
gaps.fix: Add a recall plan section or attach one. It should name the recall team and cover customer notification, public notice where needed, effectiveness checks, and how recalled product is handled.

gaps.title: No validation of the cook and cooling limits
gaps.description: Process controls must be validated with scientific evidence before or soon after the plan is put in place. The plan cites no study, reference or PCQI validation for the cook limit or the cooling limits.
gaps.fix: Put together validation evidence, such as published cook and cooling guidance or heat penetration data, and have the PCQI sign it off. Reference it in Section 7.

gaps.title: Cook limit of 212°F internal may be physically unreachable
gaps.description: Water boils at about 211.7°F at Salem's elevation, which is roughly 150 feet. Beans cooked in an open kettle likely cannot reach an internal 212°F. If so, every batch would technically miss the limit, or the logs would record a temperature that cannot be true. The weekly boiling-water thermometer check would also read slightly under 212°F.
gaps.fix: Have the PCQI set an achievable, validated cook limit, such as a stated internal temperature and hold time backed by a scientific reference. Adjust the thermometer calibration reference for local boiling point.
gaps.locator: Section 4, row 'Vegetative pathogens at cook'; Section 7
gaps.quote: Cook beans in the kettle to an internal temperature of at least 212°F for at least 60 minutes

gaps.title: Environmental monitoring and product testing procedures are incomplete
gaps.description: Environmental monitoring gives the organism, the number of sites and the frequency. It does not identify the specific sites, when during production they are swabbed, the test method, or the laboratory. Finished-product testing says monthly Listeria monocytogenes testing at an accredited lab. It gives no sampling plan, sample size, test method, named laboratory, or corrective action for a positive result.
gaps.fix: Write environmental monitoring and product testing procedures that name the sites (a site map), the timing, the number of samples, the method, the lab, and the corrective actions.
gaps.quote: Listeria spp. swabs, 10 sites weekly, zone 1 and 2

gaps.title: Calibration and test records are not reviewed
gaps.description: Records review covers the cook, cooling, sanitation, allergen and metal detection records only. Thermometer calibration, metal detector service, product testing and environmental monitoring records have no review step.
gaps.fix: Add PCQI review, within a reasonable time, of calibration, product testing and environmental monitoring records, and record who reviewed them and when.
gaps.quote: The PCQI reviews the cook, cooling, sanitation, allergen and metal detection records within seven working days of their creation.

facts.value: Refrigerated ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips in 8-oz and 16-oz sealed plastic tubs for retail
facts.quote: produces refrigerated ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips
facts.affects: Makes the products ready-to-eat and refrigerated, so Listeria environmental monitoring and refrigeration controls apply.

facts.quote: for retail sale in Oregon, Washington and Idaho
facts.affects: Interstate sale puts the plant firmly under FDA jurisdiction and shapes the reach of any recall.
Well under 500 employees, so the plant counts as a small business under Part 117.
A long refrigerated shelf life raises the Listeria growth risk and the need for a C. botulinum evaluation.

facts.quote: Products are labeled with the allergen statement "Contains: sesame" for all hummus items.
facts.affects: Requires allergen labeling and cross-contact controls for sesame, a major allergen since 2023.

scan.confidence_notes: The file read cleanly on all 7 pages. Identity came from page 1: the title, the Salem address, the effective date of May 12, 2025, the preparer and PCQI, and the unnamed approver. Company facts came from page 2. I am confident in the gaps that repeat earlier findings; each one ties directly to text in the plan or to a missing section, checked against 21 CFR 117 Subparts C and G. Two findings are new. The claim that the 212°F cook limit is unreachable is my own inference from Salem's elevation and the boiling point of water; the PCQI should confirm it. The gap on reviewing calibration and test records is read directly from Section 7. Whether C. botulinum and pH need a control depends on the formulation, which the plan does not give. The reanalysis date is worked out from the effective date plus 3 years, not stated in the plan. The registration and licensing items are based on what similar companies hold and were not checked for this company.

WILLAMETTE VALLEY FOODS, INC.
FOOD SAFETY PLAN
Ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips
Salem Plant, 1850 Fairgrounds Road NE, Salem, Oregon 97301
Effective date: May 12, 2025
Prepared by: Dana Whitfield, Quality Manager, Preventive Controls Qualified Individual
(PCQI certificate, FSPCA course, March 2024)
Approved by: Plant Manager
1. Facility and product description
Willamette Valley Foods produces refrigerated ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips in 8-ounce and 16-
ounce sealed plastic tubs for retail sale in Oregon, Washington and Idaho. The Salem plant operates one
shift, five days a week, with 28 production employees. Products are made from cooked chickpeas or black
beans, tahini, lemon juice, garlic, olive oil, salt and spices, blended, filled, sealed, coded and held
refrigerated at or below 41°F. Shelf life is 45 days refrigerated. Products are labeled with the allergen
statement "Contains: sesame" for all hummus items.
2. Process flow
Receiving of dry beans, tahini and other ingredients → dry storage or refrigerated storage → soaking and
cooking of beans (kettle, 212°F, 60 minutes minimum) → cooling in the blast chiller → blending with
other ingredients → filling and sealing → date coding → metal detection → refrigerated storage →
shipping.
3. Hazard analysis

beans (Salmonella, Listeria monocytogenes) product

4. Preventive controls
Hazard Preventive control Type Critical limit or parameter
Vegetative Cook beans in the kettle to an internal temperature of at Process Minimum 212°F for 60 minutes, measured
pathogens at cook least 212°F for at least 60 minutes with a calibrated probe thermometer

growth at cooling and to 41°F within a further 4 hours in the blast chiller 4 hours
Listeria in the Sanitation of food-contact surfaces before each Sanitation ATP swab pass before start-up; Listeria
RTE environment production run and between products; environmental spp. swabs, 10 sites weekly, zone 1 and 2
monitoring swabs weekly
Sesame allergen Allergen labeling review for every label at receipt and at Allergen Label matches the formulation sheet;
printing; product scheduling with hummus items last in washdown verified by ATP swab before
the day, followed by full washdown the next non-sesame product
Metal Metal detection of every sealed tub Process Reject at 2.0 mm ferrous, 2.5 mm non-
ferrous, 3.0 mm stainless test pieces
5. Monitoring
The kettle operator records the internal temperature and the time at the start and end of each cook batch
on the cook log. The blast chiller operator records the temperature at 2 hours and at 6 hours on the cooling
log. The sanitation lead records the ATP swab result before each start-up. The line lead runs the three
metal test pieces through the detector at start-up, every two hours, and at the end of the run, and records
the result. The quality technician reviews every label lot against the formulation sheet at receipt and signs
the label log.
6. Corrective actions
If a cook batch does not reach 212°F for 60 minutes, the batch is re-cooked to the critical limit or
discarded, and the cause is recorded. If cooling exceeds the time limits, the batch is discarded. If an ATP
swab fails, the surface is re-cleaned and re-swabbed before production starts. If a Listeria spp. swab is
positive, the site is cleaned and re-swabbed, adjacent sites are added, and product made on that line since
the last negative swab is held pending investigation. If the metal detector fails a test piece, all product
since the last passing test is re-run through the detector. If a label does not match the formulation, the lot
is quarantined and not used. All corrective actions are recorded on the corrective action log and reviewed
by the PCQI within seven days.
7. Verification
The PCQI reviews the cook, cooling, sanitation, allergen and metal detection records within seven
working days of their creation. Probe thermometers are calibrated in ice water and boiling water weekly,
and the metal detector is serviced by the manufacturer annually. Finished product is tested for Listeria
monocytogenes monthly by an accredited laboratory. Environmental monitoring results are trended
quarterly.
8. Supply-chain program
Tahini and dry beans are received only from approved suppliers who provide a current third-party audit
certificate and a certificate of analysis for each lot. The approved supplier list is maintained by the quality
manager.
9. Records
All records named in this plan are kept at the Salem plant for at least two years from the date of the record
and are available to FDA and the Oregon Department of Agriculture on request. Records are reviewed and
signed by the PCQI as described in section 7.
10. Training
All production employees receive food hygiene training at hire and annually. The PCQI holds a current
FSPCA certificate. Sanitation and line leads are trained on the monitoring procedures in this plan.

Add matching corrective actions for a wrong label on product and a failed changeover. / 21 CFR 117.135(c)(2); 21 CFR 117.145 / https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-117.145 / Section 4 (Sesame allergen row) and Section 5, Monitoring / read / The quality technician reviews every label lot against the formulation sheet at receipt and signs the label log. / 55d66a57-b6ed-4d2e-a4c0-2db70bc0f4a9

no-false-pcqi-gap.detail: not raised as such; 4 item(s) mention it — read below

soft.text: No reanalysis schedule or triggers / The plan does not say it will be reanalyzed at least every 3 years. It also does not name the events that call for a reanalysis sooner: a change in product, process, ingredient or supplier, new hazard information, an unanticipated problem, or a control that is found not to work. / Add a reanalysis section with the 3-year cycle, the triggering events, and who (the PCQI) performs or oversees it. / 21 CFR 117.170 / https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-117.170 / not in the document / read / 4dd8efe3-a783-4e4f-b6ad-893357a6e036

No validation of the cook and cooling limits / Process controls must be validated with scientific evidence before or soon after the plan is put in place. The plan cites no study, reference or PCQI validation for the cook limit or the cooling limits. / Put together validation evidence, such as published cook and cooling guidance or heat penetration data, and have the PCQI sign it off. Reference it in Section 7. / 21 CFR 117.160 / https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-117.160 / Section 7, Verification (not addressed) / read / b978eb97-5bdd-4862-9042-42fca50c8f5a

Cook limit of 212°F internal may be physically unreachable / Water boils at about 211.7°F at Salem's elevation, which is roughly 150 feet. Beans cooked in an open kettle likely cannot reach an internal 212°F. If so, every batch would technically miss the limit, or the logs would record a temperature that cannot be true. The weekly boiling-water thermometer check would also read slightly under 212°F. / Have the PCQI set an achievable, validated cook limit, such as a stated internal temperature and hold time backed by a scientific reference. Adjust the thermometer calibration reference for local boiling point. / 21 CFR 117.135(c)(1); 21 CFR 117.160 / https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-117.160 / Section 4, row 'Vegetative pathogens at cook'; Section 7 / inferred / Cook beans in the kettle to an internal temperature of at least 212°F for at least 60 minutes

Calibration and test records are not reviewed / Records review covers the cook, cooling, sanitation, allergen and metal detection records only. Thermometer calibration, metal detector service, product testing and environmental monitoring records have no review step. / Add PCQI review, within a reasonable time, of calibration, product testing and environmental monitoring records, and record who reviewed them and when. / 21 CFR 117.165(a)(4)(ii) / https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-117.165 / Section 7, Verification / read / The PCQI reviews the cook, cooling, sanitation, allergen and metal detection records within seven working days of their creation.

soft.text: Supply-chain program is missing required elements / The section is two sentences long. It does not say which hazards the suppliers control. It does not explain how suppliers are approved, how the verification activities and their frequency were chosen, or how certificates of analysis are checked. It covers no ingredients beyond tahini and beans, and it does not list the supply-chain records to be kept. / Write out the program: which ingredients have supplier-controlled hazards, how suppliers are approved, the chosen verification activities and why, and how to receive from approved suppliers only. Include the records kept under 117.475. / 21 CFR 117.405, 117.410, 117.415, 117.420, 117.430, 117.475 / https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/part-117/subpart-G / Section 8, Supply-chain program / read / Tahini and dry beans are received only from approved suppliers who provide a current third-party audit certificate and a certificate of analysis for each lot. / a7162bce-ac53-4593-9560-9662659bfbb3

no-false-monitoring-gap.detail: not raised as such; 5 item(s) mention it — read below

soft.text: Stones in dry beans have no working control / The hazard analysis says stones in dry beans are controlled by metal detection and supplier screening. A metal detector does not find stones. Supplier screening is not written up as a supply-chain control, and no monitoring or verification is set for it. / Add a working control for stones, such as a destoner or visual sorting at receiving or soaking, with monitoring and corrective actions. Or write up the supplier screening as a supply-chain-applied control with verification under Subpart G. / 21 CFR 117.130; 21 CFR 117.135 / https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-117/subpart-C / Section 3, Hazard analysis, row 'Receiving dry beans' / read / Field debris in dry beans, controlled at metal detection and by supplier screening / 02a830b6-0ae3-4206-bc05-18ba46d06e57

Corrective actions leave out required steps / Most corrective actions only deal with the product. They do not say how the cause will be found and fixed, how a repeat will be prevented, or how affected food will be evaluated and kept out of commerce. Examples: cooling failure, ATP failure, metal detector failure, label mismatch. There is also no corrective action for a positive finished-product Listeria test, and none for an unanticipated problem. / For each control, add these steps: find and correct the cause, prevent a repeat, evaluate affected food, and keep adulterated food out of commerce. Add a procedure for a positive product test and a general procedure under 117.150(b) for problems the plan does not anticipate. / 21 CFR 117.150(a)(2) and 117.150(b) / https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-117.150 / Section 6, Corrective actions / read / If cooling exceeds the time limits, the batch is discarded. / 16243ee2-8dff-4e2d-a5ea-d220478fb31b

Label check at packaging is not monitored, and neither are allergen changeovers / The allergen control calls for label review at receipt and at printing, plus a washdown checked by ATP swab before the next product without sesame. Monitoring covers only the label review at receipt. Nothing checks that the right label is on the right product at filling or coding. Nothing records the scheduling order or the washdown and ATP result at the sesame changeover. / Add monitoring for the label check at packaging or start-up and for each changeover washdown, with the ATP result. Add matching corrective actions for a wrong label on product and a failed changeover. / 21 CFR 117.135(c)(2); 21 CFR 117.145 / https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-117.145 / Section 4 (Sesame allergen row) and Section 5, Monitoring / read / The quality technician reviews every label lot against the formulation sheet at receipt and signs the label log. / 55d66a57-b6ed-4d2e-a4c0-2db70bc0f4a9

Cold storage is listed as needing a control, but there is no control, monitoring or corrective action / The hazard analysis marks Listeria growth in refrigerated storage as needing a preventive control. Section 4 has no storage temperature control, Section 5 has no cooler temperature monitoring, and Section 6 has no corrective action for a temperature excursion. / Add a refrigeration control (41°F or below), continuous or scheduled cooler temperature monitoring, and corrective actions for excursions, with the product held and evaluated. / 21 CFR 117.135(c)(1), 117.145, 117.150 / https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-117.135 / Section 3, row 'Refrigerated storage'; missing from Sections 4–6 / read / Refrigerated RTE product with a 45-day shelf life / 80b2cdf1-00a3-462a-9c86-137b4a782f63

Environmental monitoring and product testing procedures are incomplete / Environmental monitoring gives the organism, the number of sites and the frequency. It does not identify the specific sites, when during production they are swabbed, the test method, or the laboratory. Finished-product testing says monthly Listeria monocytogenes testing at an accredited lab. It gives no sampling plan, sample size, test method, named laboratory, or corrective action for a positive result. / Write environmental monitoring and product testing procedures that name the sites (a site map), the timing, the number of samples, the method, the lab, and the corrective actions. / 21 CFR 117.165(a)(2)–(3) and 117.165(b)(2)–(3) / https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-117.165 / Section 4 (Listeria row) and Section 7 / read / Listeria spp. swabs, 10 sites weekly, zone 1 and 2 / d7062715-930f-4176-b3f9-e220d9ac75aa
